articles.title: Paraguay President Santiago Peña resigns after bank collapse
articles.summary: The move follows a bank collapse and after the lower house of congress voted in favour of pursuing an impeachment trial against him.
articles.body:
Paraguay's President Santiago Peña has announced his resignation following a political crisis sparked by the collapse of a bank linked to him.

"I want to apologise to the people if at any point I failed," he said in a video message on social media. "It was never my intention to betray the trust you placed in me."

The crisis erupted after Ueno Bank entered an insolvency process, which froze all operations. Lawmakers accused Peña, who was a shareholder until last year in the company that owned the bank, of conflicts of interest and misconduct.

Peña has rejected suggestions of impropriety. His resignation comes after Paraguay's lower house of congress voted in favour of pursuing an impeachment trial.

In his video message posted on X, Peña said his resignation was to protect stability, social peace and democratic institutions.

Ueno Bank has said it has about three million customers, equivalent to about 60% of Paraguay's adult population.

It held pensions and some other public funds and, after its collapse earlier this week, millions could not access their accounts.

The central bank seized the digital lender, and people took to the streets protesting and demanding Peña's resignation.

A new president of the Central Bank of Paraguay has been appointed and Congress has approved a process to pay depositors.

Peña won election in 2023 representing Paraguay's ruling conservative Colorado Party, beating a centre-left challenger.

articles.title: Disarm Hezbollah, but don’t let it cash in on Lebanon’s reconstruction
articles.summary: While Washington is right to make disarmament a prerequisite, it is wrong to make it the only one.
articles.body:
Last month, the State Department set out the terms on which Lebanon can expect help rebuilding after two wars with Israel. “Billions of dollars can be injected into Lebanon,” said spokesperson Tommy Pigott, “but only after Hezbollah’s disarmament.”

While Washington is right to make disarmament a prerequisite, it is wrong to make it the only one.

Lebanon needs the money. Prime Minister Nawaf Salam has told parliament that losses from Israel’s wars since 2023 could exceed $27 billion, and the World Bank expects the economy to shrink 6.4 percent this year. Visiting the bombed-out city of Nabatiyeh on Oct. 2, Salam conceded that rebuilding the south is beyond the state’s means.

But recovery relies on three settlements: First, Hezbollah’s weapons; second, who absorbs the roughly $70 billion in losses from the 2019 banking collapse; and third, who controls the reconstruction money. American terms only address the first of the three. The other two will determine whether aid rebuilds the Lebanese state or sustains the patronage networks that hollowed it out.

Seven years after the crash, Lebanon still has no functioning credit system. The gap law , which would divide the losses among the state, the central bank, commercial banks and depositors, has stalled in a parliament that extended its own term to 2028. The International Monetary Fund has made the law — along with a 2027 budget and medium-term fiscal plan — a condition for any new program.

Creative stopgaps like the Salim Khalil mechanism , which routes legitimate dollar transactions through regulated institutions and has held the Lebanese pound to near 89,500 to the dollar since 2023, buy time. They do not substitute for reform.

Without working banks, reconstruction runs on cash. Families in the South of Lebanon will rebuild with grants and not mortgages or insurance payouts — and whoever hands these out collects the political credit.

After the 2024 war, Hezbollah’s construction arm, Jihad al-Binaa, paid an estimated $400 million to affected families, more than the World Bank’s $250 million emergency loan . Since August 2025, the state has channeled about $132 million through the Council for South Lebanon, a body exempt from prior audit and closely tied to Parliament Speaker Nabih Berri’s Amal movement, Hezbollah’s ally.

Lebanon has been here before. After the civil war, the state borrowed heavily to rebuild, while former warlords, amnestied and back in government, divided contracts and public jobs among their followers. Lebanese banks financed the state’s debt with depositors’ money and, by early 2020, held $12.7 billion of the roughly $30 billion in outstanding Eurobonds. When dollar inflows dried up in March 2020, the state defaulted on its debt, turning the banks’ losses into the depositors’ losses — which the gap law must now address.

A deal that trades Hezbollah’s heavy weapons for Gulf money, while leaving the banks unresolved and the cash economy intact, would repeat that mistake. Hezbollah might lose its arsenal but keep its financial networks, including the unlicensed lender al-Qard al-Hassan that is vital to its community and influence.

The disarmament track is itself fragile. Under the June 26 U.S.-brokered framework , the Lebanese army has to clear weapons from “pilot zones” while Israel withdraws. Fewer than 10 percent of residents had returned to Zawtar al-Gharbiyeh, the first zone, by August. Israel is threatening a new campaign over reports that Hezbollah is rearming, and United Nations peacekeepers begin withdrawing after Dec. 31. If reconstruction waits until full disarmament, the South may suffer for years, and Hezbollah will fill the vacuum.

As the World Bank’s largest shareholder and the Lebanese army’s main donor , the U.S. has the leverage to do better. Congress, which funds that army and oversees the U.S. vote at the World Bank, can write that leverage into appropriations. Three changes would help.

First, add financial benchmarks to the security benchmarks. Large-scale reconstruction funds should be contingent on the passage of an International Monetary Fund-approved gap law, as well as on verified disarmament. That would put the cost of delay on the parliamentary blocs causing it.

Second, separate emergency recovery from disarmament. Shelter, water networks and hospitals cannot wait for verification teams. If the Lebanese state does not deliver them this winter, Jihad al-Binaa will.

Third, insist that any reconstruction funds flow through accountable state channels — a public damage registry, direct applications from households, electronic tenders and a single verification body for all donors. Salam has made a start here, with 23 public tenders for debris removal, roads and hospital equipment in Nabatiyeh.

Lebanon has its most reform-minded leadership in decades, and Hezbollah is currently debilitated. This creates a real but narrow opening.

Lebanon’s friends in Washington and elsewhere should not make disarmament, however critical, the only demand of a political system still captured by entrenched interests. Otherwise, Lebanon may see calm on its border and some reconstruction, while the losses of 2019 go unresolved and a sprawling cash economy enables Hezbollah’s regeneration. That would be another reconstruction of the old order, financed this time by Gulf grants instead of Eurobonds.

Patricia Karam is a non-resident fellow at the Arab Center Washington DC and a senior advisor at the Middle East Institute. She previously served as vice president of policy at the American Task Force on Lebanon.

articles.title: Bomb threats have disrupted more than 20 flights across Europe this week. Here’s what we know
articles.summary: More than 20 flights across Europe have been impacted by a string of hoax bomb threats this week, disrupting travel plans and in some cases forcing countries to scramble fighter jets.
articles.body: More than 20 flights across Europe have been impacted by a string of hoax bomb threats this week, disrupting travel plans and in some cases forcing countries to scramble fighter jets. Over a dozen flights were impacted on Thursday, including four flight diversions in the Czech Republic and two in Italy. It is the second day of widespread flight disruption due to bomb threats this week. On Tuesday, at least seven flights and one cruise ship received bomb threats. Here’s what we know so far. How were the threats made? It’s not completely clear, although Czech and Italian authorities say they were made by email. A representative of Václav Havel Airport in Prague, told CNN the threats it received about bombs being placed on four flights were made in an anonymous email. A Czech Police spokesperson told CNN the email was addressed to the airport, adding that similar emails were sent to other airports in Europe. The Italy flight threats came in an email from an anti-feminist group calling itself “The Male State” to a logistics hub company working with Rome Fiumicino Airport. The email, first published by CNN Affiliate SkyTG24, made the false claim that “explosive devices” had been placed on two flights - one from Helsinki and another from Dublin. A spokesperson for the airport confirmed to CNN the screenshot was authentic. The International Centre for Counter-Terrorism, a Netherlands-based think tank, said “The Male State,” was created in Russia in 2016 as a misogynist movement, that later emerged as a vocal supporter of the Ukraine war. A Russian court banned the group and labelled it as an extremist organization in 2021. All European airports plan and carry out training for incidents like these. Speaking to CNN, Keith Jeffries, a former Federal Security Director at LAX airport, said that all airports “will have bomb threat management plans, and they’ll train to that plan,” allowing them to make decisions in a matter of seconds. The bottom line is that no aviation authority will ever ignore a bomb threat, Jeffries said. Who was behind it? Again, it remains unclear at this stage who exactly was behind the threats. No official group or state has been identified by any European country at this stage. The European Union has said it is too early to say whether the incidents are linked. Security analysts have suggested it could be part of a wider hybrid campaign or series of malicious hoaxes. Eric Schouten, the head of aviation security group Dyami, suggested saboteurs acting on behalf of the Russian state could be to blame. “From railways to the food infrastructure that you see happening with the fridges being hacked ⁠and all ​kinds of other operations, it does fit the narrative of Russian state actors ​who want to disturb Europe,” Schouten said, according to Reuters. He also pointed out that many of the countries affected have supported Ukraine in its war with Russia. The UK’s transport minister described the threats as a “malicious hoax.” Speaking to British media, Heidi Alexander said that the disrupted flights had triggered “established processes for dealing with hoax and malicious threats, and that’s what these threats have been.” What’s the impact been? Overall, the impact has been relatively contained. All the threats have so far proven false, with the authorities involved saying that no such explosive devices have been found. They have, of course, caused disruption to travelers. The passengers and crew on at least 14 planes were impacted on Thursday, including an Aer Lingus flight bound for Rome that was diverted to France and two flights from Spain and Denmark that were forced to divert to Bulgarian capital Sofia. It comes after at least seven flights were rerouted on Tuesday. Analysts are warning the threats could be aimed at both causing disruption and observing the response from airlines and authorities. “These aviation threats are also occurring in the same period as cyberattacks on supermarket refrigeration systems across Europe,” Eliran Almog, CEO of aviation cybersecurity firm Cyviation, told Reuters. “Different essential services are experiencing disruption that carries economic costs and can undermine public confidence.”

articles.title: Vance lances Trump as MAGA enters week of the long knives
articles.summary: TOI correspondent from Washington: There were no hidden Trump voters, just angry Trump voters, standing in plain sight, carrying their grievances to the
articles.body: TOI correspondent from Washington: There were no hidden Trump voters, just angry Trump voters, standing in plain sight, carrying their grievances to the ballot box and voting for Democrats because they were upset about the Iran war. In essence, that was US vice president JD Vance's explosive explanation for the Republican Party's electoral debacle in a post in which he appeared to throw his boss under the bus while positioning himself to run for the White House in 2028.In what was a quick 614-word post-mortem of the Republican rout even as final tallies are still being tabulated, Vance argued that strategists had been looking in the wrong place, obsessing over turnout when the real problem was that Trump-Vance voters from 2024 were switching sides. His data analysts had been reassured by turnout figures, but one particularly astute pollster had warned that many former Republican voters were angry and planning to vote Democrat. Their grievances, Vance said, boiled down to four demands: end the war, tackle inflation and the cost of living, put America First, and change America's relationship with Israel. "The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night," Vance wrote, glossing over the fact that his boss initiated the war and he was implicitly a party to it.In fact, Vance had previously defended the military action and served as a prominent administration spokesman. But now, with the electoral wreckage still smoldering, political pundits saw him positioning himself as the man who understood the voters' anger -- and perhaps the man who could lead the party out of the rubble. The 2028 subtext was not exactly written in invisible ink.Asked for his reaction to Vance's assessment, Trump said it was "largely true," conceding that the war had pushed up gasoline prices and hurt Republicans. But he insisted he would do it all over again, arguing that preventing Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon left him with no choice. He also does have another election to win.Vance, meanwhile, was already drawing boundaries around the post-Trump Republican Party with his election autopsy that doubled as a campaign manifesto: less foreign intervention, greater economic populism, tougher immigration enforcement and a reassessment of the relationship with Israel. His warning against an amnesty-driven response to the defeat was a pre-emptive strike against Republicans who might use the results to advocate softer immigration policies.Already, leaked stories suggest there has been some bloodletting on the issue even in the White House, with reports that Stephen Miller, architect of Trump's hard-line immigration program, was on the backfoot after Melania Trump expressed unhappiness with the scale and consequences of the deportation drive. According to one account, she had complained that people she knew were being caught up in the crackdown, prompting Trump to tell aides that enforcement should concentrate more on criminals rather than indiscriminate deportation targets.Meanwhile, while Democrats were dancing downtown at the unexpected electoral sweep, the knives were out in the GOP ranks. Marjorie Taylor Greene, once among Trump's most ardent cheerleaders before their spectacular falling-out, declared that Republicans would have to "kick Donald Trump out" if the party wanted a future. She accused him of turning the GOP into a warmongering, corporate-focused outfit that had abandoned the conservative values of its voters.Conservative commentator Matt Walsh called the Iran war the greatest political blunder in at least two decades, describing it as an "unforgivable betrayal of America First principles" and demanding new Republican leadership, while Nebraska Republican Don Bacon blamed the administration's tariffs and broader political conduct for alienating voters, arguing that Americans disliked "chaos, narcissism, tariffs, corruption" and arrogance.Elsewhere, Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth was discovering that the Pentagon's most dangerous battlefield is the White House personnel office, with reports that Trump was privately asking advisors whether the machismo-infused war hawk should remain in his job. While Trump publicly defended Hegseth, saying he was doing a "very good job", and the White House insisted he retained the president's confidence, many previous cabinet officials can attest that the MAGA boss’ endorsements can have a remarkably short shelf life.And then there was Trump himself, whose response to the electoral earthquake was perhaps the most extraordinary spectacle. His normally prolific Truth Social output was relatively subdued, apart from blaming Republican candidates and taking a swipe at Fox News. Instead, he appeared more interested in construction than political reconstruction. At a White House appearance, he celebrated the installation of what he described as the final steel beam for his proposed ballroom, holding forth on limestone pillars, Corinthian columns, marble floors and chandeliers.There was something almost impressively tone-deaf about the spectacle: Voters had just delivered a drubbing to his party, wanting lower prices, but the MAGA boss was busy discussing higher ceilings.You use AI every day. articles.title: Russell Brand found guilty of rape and sexual assault
articles.summary: Brand is told to expect a prison sentence "of some length" and faces more rape allegations, it can now be reported.
articles.body:
Russell Brand has been convicted of rape and sexual assault, and is now expected to face a substantial prison sentence.

A jury found the entertainer guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault, following a four-week trial at Southwark Crown Court in London.

He was found not guilty of two other counts of rape, and one count of attempted indecent assault. The jury deliberated for eight-and-a-half hours.

Brand was taken into custody after the verdicts were delivered, and was refused bail. He is due to be sentenced on Monday.

It can now be reported that Brand is also facing further rape allegations made by two women and the 51-year-old has already been questioned by officers in relation to the complaints. The Metropolitan Police said its investigation "remains ongoing".

During the trial, Brand faced allegations from six women spanning the decade between 1999 and 2009, when he rose to fame as one of Britain's most high-profile entertainers.

The women came to court to reveal how Brand used his immense fame to force them into sexual activity.

Brand, who told his wife Laura Brand "I love you" after entering the dock, displayed no emotion as the jury delivered its verdicts.

Afterwards he mouthed "I'm good, I'm good" to his defence counsel as he left the dock. His walk was steadily paced, and he continued to show little emotion.

The judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, told Brand to expect "a significant custodial term" after the verdicts were delivered.

The jury found Brand guilty of raping a fan after meeting her at a 2009 stand-up show at the Hammersmith Apollo.

Brand was found guilty of groping an MTV worker during a party at a Soho bar in 2004, but not guilty of going on to rape her in a toilet.

He was convicted of kissing and groping a Choice FM worker after encountering her in a corridor at the Capital Radio building in 2004 or 2005.

Brand was also convicted by the jury of sexually assaulting a Channel 4 worker in 2009 when she had been forced to give him a massage.

Brand was found not guilty by the jury of raping a woman he met at a cabaret show on the fringes of the 1999 Labour Party conference in Bournemouth.

He was also cleared of trying to drag an MTV worker in to a toilet to indecently assault her in 2001.

Brand had claimed to be the victim of a media conspiracy to paint him as a sexual predator and insisted in court that consent was "more important than sex itself".

But he faced the compelling evidence of six women who accused him of crimes over the course of a decade.

Brand was also confronted with his own words from his 2007 book in which he claimed sex was a "birthright" and friends who revealed his relentless pursuit of sleeping with 5,000 women.

Mr Justice Bennathan ruled that Brand must be remanded into custody until sentencing on Monday, when he is expected to receive a lengthy prison sentence.

The judge said "I regret the hardship caused to the children, of course" after being told that Brand would like bail over the weekend to explain the convictions to his children.

But he said Brand "has considerable resources", adding: "Whatever the good intentions of the family and the defendant today, I think there are substantial grounds to fear he might in the end not feel able to come along and face his sentence."

After the verdict, Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy paid tribute to the "extraordinary courage, resilience and determination of the women who came forward and reported what happened to them".

"Despite intense media and public scrutiny, they relived deeply personal and traumatic experiences and placed their trust in us. Without their bravery, this outcome would not have been possible," he said.

"Brand used his influence, status and fame to exploit and sexually offend against women. As his profile grew, so too did his sense of entitlement."

He added: "I hope this conviction sends a clear message that no one is above the law, no matter how famous or powerful they may be."

David Roberts, senior crown prosecutor in the London rape and serious sexual assault unit, described Brand as "predatory".

"He was a manipulator with an insatiable desire to get what he wanted regardless of whether consent was given or not," he said.

"As his career took off, he seized opportunities to assault the women around him. Although his tactics varied, at the centre of every assault was an abuse of power and sexual greed, with a complete disregard for the impact of his actions.

Ron Brand, Russell's father told the BBC he was "bemused and shocked" by the verdicts, adding: "I just didn't expect this - it's wrong... it's devastating."

In his evidence, Brand admitted using his fame to "facilitate sexual access" and being "obsessed" with sex and "extremely promiscuous" in the past.

He said he had "dedicated a lot of my life to what seems now beyond reckless, philandering, and idiocy".

But he insisted the sex was always consensual, and he denied all the charges.

His barrister told jurors that Brand "had an immense amount of sex", but that "none of it was unlawful".

Allegations about Brand's behaviour first emerged in the media in September 2023.

The Times, Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches programme jointly reported that four women had accused him of rape, sexual assault and emotional abuse - claims he strongly denied.

The investigation into other reports against Brand began soon after the story broke.

Brand first rose to fame as a stand-up comedian and became a household name as host of TV shows such as Big Brother's Big Mouth, and with his own radio programmes on stations including BBC Radio 2 and 6 Music.

He went on to establish a Hollywood career, starring in films including Forgetting Sarah Marshall and Get Him To The Greek. He was married to pop star Katy Perry from 2010 to 2012.

In recent years he has reinvented himself as an online social, political and religious commentator.

Channel 4, The Times and Sunday Times and the BBC all paid tribute to the women involved in the case, highlighting their "courage".

Channel 4, which aired Big Brother and its spin-off programmes at the time Brand was a presenter, said it recognised the "profound impact of these crimes".

The Times and The Sunday Times also paid tribute to women who took part in their investigation with Channel 4 but who did not have their cases brought before a court, saying their contributions had been "vital".

A BBC spokesperson said there could be "no place for the abuse of power" and added: "Across the industry we must work together to ensure that anyone who suffers at someone else's hand feels able to report it, that their concerns are taken seriously and that they are listened to."

The corporation restated its apology to staff who felt they could not speak up with concerns about Brand's behaviour when he worked at the BBC between 2006 and 2008, because he was seen as "too influential".

articles.title: Skewen pays tribute to Bonnie Tyler with new mural
articles.summary: Artist Steve Jenkins painted the "important" piece at Skewen Memorial Park, in Neath Port Talbot.
articles.body:
A mural of Bonnie Tyler has been unveiled in her hometown as a tribute to the global star "who never forgot her roots".

The Holding Out For a Hero singer, whose real name was Gaynor Hopkins, died in a hospital in Portugal in July , aged 75, after undergoing emergency intestinal surgery earlier this year.

Hundreds lined the streets of Skewen , in Neath Port Talbot, where she was born and raised, to pay their respects on the day of her funeral.

Artist Steve Jenkins, who painted the piece at Skewen Memorial Park, said it was "important" and the "pressure was on" to get the artwork right for the community.

The mural features a large picture of Tyler's face, as well as references to the local rugby club and Total Eclipse of the Heart - one of her best-known hits.

Speaking to BBC Wales, walkers passing the mural described the tribute as "fantastic".

Susan Petrosillo, 61, from Skewen, said she was "very, very proud".

"It's absolutely fantastic what they've done. It's such a lovely park as well," she said.

"She was such a big part of Skewen and still is."

On 17 August, a celebration of life service was held at Swansea Minster ahead of a private family funeral in the village.

Petrosillo added: "On the day of her funeral, the hearse came through Skewen and the amount of people who came out for that was amazing."

For those who grew up alongside her, like Michael Davies, the mural is a chance to remember someone they knew long before she became a global superstar.

"I was in school with her, so I did know her quite well," he said.

"She was a Skewen girl, so it's tremendous."

Bob Marney, 84, said the reference to the local rugby club - an emblem in the corner of the painting - was particularly significant.

"The rugby club is where she had her first audition," he said.

"She's a legend. She was down to earth, never forgot her roots. She never forgot Skewen."

For artist Jenkins, capturing Tyler's likeness came with "huge responsibility".

"I knew that I had to get it really accurate because of the emotions tied with Bonnie," he said.

"I knew that the family and the whole community were going to get quite emotional about seeing this, so it was important. The pressure was on."

Jenkins, known as Jenks Art, said the design evolved several times before reaching its final form.

"The first mock-up we had had Mumbles Lighthouse in the background," he said.

"But [with Tyler] being so proud of being from Skewen, we decided to put Skewen Park in the background."

He added the two-tone design of Tyler's face also carried a deeper meaning.

"As I was painting it, and as I was being approached by people, it became apparent that her music is going to live on.

"And that's sort of represented in the colour side of the face, and then, being a memorial piece, the black-and-white side of the face represents that."

articles.title: Two Connecticut brothers spent $30 on a box of football cards and found a one-of-a-kind Tom Brady collectible with odds estimated at one in 10.5 million; the card is headed to auction with a minimum valuation of $150,000
articles.summary: Lucas, 23, and Trevor Martell, 18, bought three $30 boxes of Topps NFL Bowman cards from a Target store on October 15. Each brother took one for himself.
articles.body: Lucas, 23, and Trevor Martell, 18, bought three $30 boxes of Topps NFL Bowman cards from a Target store on October 15. Each brother took one for himself. They agreed to open the third together in the car.Once they got into the car, they opened the third box and saw something they never expected. The card was a one-of-one Garbage Pail Kids SuperFractor featuring Tom Brady, with a gold border and gold lettering! Lucas could tell it was special before he read the name. “We kind of, like, lost it right then and there,” Lucas told the New Haven Register.One in 10.5 million chanceWhat are the chances of pulling this card? Well, let’s just say they're one in 10.5 million, and most people will never open a pack that holds anything close to it. The card is so rare because it is the only copy that exists. It comes from a collaboration between Garbage Pail Kids and Topps, and a similar one-of-one Garbage Pail Kids SuperFractor of Cooper Flagg sold for $288,000, which Topps says is the most expensive Garbage Pail Kids card ever sold. Brady’s name adds further value to the card. Brady cards have sold for millions, and recent Brady SuperFractors have reached the mid-six figures at Fanatics auctions.That’s not all they found. “Right behind that card, there was a Drake Maye, it's called the Etched in Glass, and that card's worth like $200 itself,” Lucas Martell told the outlet.A recent hobby that brought the fortuneLucas only recently took up the hobby of collecting sports cards. Trevor has been collecting for much longer. The brothers started visiting shops to learn more about the hobby, and that led them to Treasure Chest of Mystic in Olde Mistick Village, a new store. The owner, Carmine Lorusso, became a friend of the brothers. He walked them through the process of getting the card into an auction run by Fanatics Collect.The card is heading for Fanatics Collect’s Premier Auction, which opens on November 5 and closes on November 14. Under the agreement, Lucas will receive 115% of the final winning bid! The company describes that figure as the full sale price plus 75% of the auction house’s 20% buyer’s premium. Fanatics also offered an advance of up to half the card’s minimum estimated value. That value rests on an underlying valuation of at least $150,000, and the company says the final price could be much higher. The card has been insured for $350,000 during shipping to Los Angeles and will be graded by Beckett Grading Services before being placed in a vault to await the sale.For the brothers, the money will change their lives in practical ways. Lucas has large medical bills following an emergency room visit, as he did not have proper insurance. His Jeep also needs repairs. After those debts are paid, he wants to help his grandmother.After that, the brothers have bigger plans. They want to start their own trading card business, where they can enjoy the hobby and buy and sell cards with other collectors. Lucas said Trevor would get a fair share of the money, as the two of them are in it together. "Just have, like, our own name for it and, so since he was with me, he's definitely going to get a good cut out of the money because we're pretty much in this together."You use AI every day. articles.title: Iran says tankers struck in Hormuz amid fears of new US attack
articles.summary: Iranian forces say five oil tankers and a tugboat have caught fire in several incidents in the Strait of Hormuz.
articles.body:
At least five tankers have been damaged in the Strait of Hormuz, Iranian forces said, making clear that shipping would remain in peril as long as the United States and Israel’s war on the country is unresolved.

Since the war on Iran began in late February, Tehran has severely restricted traffic through the strategic waterway, which normally carries about one-fifth of global oil consumption.

“Last night … a large oil tanker attempting to pass through the illegal passageway south of the Strait of Hormuz suffered a fire after striking a mine and was brought to a halt,” Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) told the Fars news agency on Thursday.

“Another supertanker was halted by a massive fire while exiting the eastern Strait of Hormuz. A tugboat that had approached the supertanker to extinguish the fire also caught fire,” the IRGC added.

The Iranian army later said three more tankers were hit by naval mines and caught fire.

“Early this morning, a violating oil tanker – navigating through an unsafe area east of the Strait of Hormuz – caught fire and came to a halt after striking a naval mine,” the army said, according to the official IRNA news agency.

“Today at around noon, two more oil tankers struck naval mines and caught fire in the unsafe waters east of the Strait of Hormuz,” said another army statement carried by IRNA.

Separately, the British military said a tanker was struck by two projectiles off Qatar’s coast.

The vessel was hit about 50 nautical miles (about 93 kilometres) north of Qatar’s ⁠Madinat ash-Shamal on Wednesday at 23:20 GMT, the ⁠United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said on Thursday.

UKMTO did not identify the tanker or which country’s flag it was sailing under. There was no immediate claim of responsibility for the attack.

In an incident last week, a Qatari tanker was hit by “unidentified objects” while sailing in the Gulf.

The liquefied natural gas (LNG) carrier Al Mayeda was hit on October 30, the Qatar Gas Transport Company (Nakilat) said on Sunday.

No crew members were injured, and there ‌was no environmental impact, the company said, adding that the vessel remained ‌safe and ‌operational while the impact was being assessed.

Attacks on tankers in the Gulf are still running close to a record pace.

UKMTO said in a report last month that it was “struggling to accurately report” the true number of attacks as the majority of ships now refuse to report them.

Qatar has stepped up mediation efforts to resume talks on ending the war in recent days.

Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs’ spokesperson said on Tuesday that ⁠both sides were reviewing proposals ⁠put forward by mediators, with talks continuing.

But unnamed Pentagon officials and military commanders told The New York Times on Wednesday that thousands of US air and naval forces on more than a dozen ships and at bases around the Middle East and in the US are poised to resume major combat operations against Iran on President Donald Trump’s orders.

Iranian government and military leaders, however, have warned of repercussions if the US or Israel pursue further military action.

On Wednesday, Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said there should not be “even the slightest inclination towards submission” to the US, which he said would remain hostile towards Iran no matter which party was in power.

IRGC Ground Force commander Brigadier General Mohammad Karami said on Wednesday that the continuation of “hostile and brutal actions by Iran’s enemies” would lead to “further Iranian victories and greater national pride”, while accelerating the expulsion of foreign powers from the region and the collapse of Israel.

articles.title: ‘Like a bolt from the blue’: Israel’s president shocked by Trump announcing end of aid
articles.summary: Israeli President Isaac Herzog said it was “like a bolt from the blue” when President Donald Trump announced on Tuesday, the day of the midterm elections, that he would end US aid to Israel.
articles.body: Israeli President Isaac Herzog said it was “like a bolt from the blue” when President Donald Trump announced on Tuesday, the day of the midterm elections, that he would end US aid to Israel. Herzog brought up the issue during a meeting with the Yashar party, led by Gadi Eisenkot, the main rival of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. “The issue of the American aid worries me greatly, and it also fell on me like a bolt from the blue. We have an (memorandum of understanding) with the US that is supposed to last until 2028 and this is one of the major goals, and therefore a government must be formed and not go to repeated elections,” he said. Trump said aid to Israel would end this year, two years ahead of the formal end of the memorandum of understanding (MoU), which provides Israel with $3.8 billion per year to purchase American weaponry. But he offered few details in the announcement, which was made in an Election Day phone interview with Fox News. Netanyahu has not made any public comment on the announcement. “It’s a bad talking point because when you say, ‘Why don’t we give everybody $4 billion?’ Israel’s our number one; we give them more than anybody else, and they no longer need it,” Trump told Fox. US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee said he was looking for clarification on what would happen. In an interview with Israel’s Channel 12 News, he defended military aid, which has grown increasingly unpopular in both the Democratic and Republican parties. “Americans need to know the value of the relationship,” he said. “It’s not about what Americans are putting into it. It’s about what they are getting out of it. Maybe we haven’t done a good job helping the American public to recognize and be grateful for the partnership with Israel, which has benefited their lives every day.” Huckabee also disagreed with Vice President JD Vance, who said on X that the relationship with Israel contributed to Republican losses in the midterms. A staunch support of Israel, Huckabee said, “I don’t think support for Israel is toxic in the conservative wing and the Republican Party.” A task for Herzog While Herzog navigates Trump’s announcement the US is cutting off $4 billion in aid to Israel, he faces a crucial task following elections in his own country. Eisenkot emerged with a majority of the incoming Israeli Knesset’s backing after the conclusion of the president’s meetings with the elected parties, following Israel’s election late last month. Herzog held two days of consultations with representatives of all of the parties elected to the incoming Knesset. Netanyahu secured the backing of only 46 seats after one of his ultra-Orthodox allies refused to endorse him, leaving him far short of the 61-seat majority needed. Eisenkot secured the backing of lawmakers holding 67 seats, but 19 of those are held by Arab-led parties, complicating his path to oust Israel’s longest-serving leader. Herzog must now decide who gets the mandate to form the next government, a decision he said he will make Sunday. “The results of the consultations may appear clear, but the authority vested in me by law is to determine who has the ability to form a government, and that is not entirely clear,” he said after meeting all the parties. In a statement Thursday evening, Eisenkot’s party made it clear it expects to receive the mandate to form a government. “The decision of the people and the clear parliamentary majority leave no room for doubt: Israeli citizens chose change and expressed absolute no-confidence in outgoing Prime Minister Netanyahu and his government,” the Yashar party said. Netanyahu, the statement continued, “has no mandate, no majority, and no trust of the people.” Whoever is chosen will have 28 days to negotiate with other parties over cabinet posts, budgets and policies. A 14-day extension is possible. If he fails, the mandate passes to another candidate for another four weeks. If he fails too, the Knesset gets a short window to put forward another candidate. If it cannot, the country automatically returns to the polls. Until Israel has a new government, Netanyahu will remain caretaker prime minister. Netanyahu, who lost his parliamentary majority, is still challenging the election results and claims the vote was “stolen” by Arab-led parties through bribery, foreign funding and fraud. The opposition says he is trying to delay the swearing in of the Knesset Tuesday, and to prevent plans to replace the Knesset speaker with a lawmaker from the opposition.

articles.title: California grandfather cared for his granddaughter nearly two years, then sought visits after her mother regained custody; court allowed a five-minute monthly call, and appeal upheld denial of $17,193 in legal fees
articles.summary: A grandfather who once helped raise his granddaughter for nearly two years found himself seeking court intervention to maintain contact with her after her
articles.body: A grandfather who once helped raise his granddaughter for nearly two years found himself seeking court intervention to maintain contact with her after her mother regained custody. Although he requested regular visits, family dinners and weekly video calls, the court initially allowed him only a five-minute telephone conversation with the children once a month. The dispute eventually reached California's Court of Appeal, where a separate question about legal expenses became the central issue.The ruling in Timothy S v. Sarah H, issued on November 3, 2026, by California's Court of Appeal, Fourth Appellate District, Division One, is available on Justia under case number D087153. The appeal was brought by the children's mother, who wanted the grandfather to pay $17,193 in attorney's fees and legal costs she incurred while opposing his visitation petition. The appellate court upheld the lower court's refusal to award the money, explaining that the law governing attorney's fees in parentage proceedings did not apply to a separate petition for grandparent visitation.Grandfather sought regular visits after helping raise his granddaughterThe dispute involved two children, S.S. and J.S., born in 2018 and 2021 to Sarah H and T.S., the grandfather's son. The couple were never married. In September 2019, when the older child was approximately 17 months old, authorities removed her from her parents' custody and placed her with her paternal grandfather, Timothy S, and his wife. Sarah regained custody of the child in August 2021.When the juvenile court later ended its involvement in the children's cases, it issued final custody and visitation orders. Sarah received sole physical custody of both children, along with shared legal custody with their father. The father was also granted supervised visitation. However, the grandfather wanted to maintain his relationship with the children. In April 2024, he filed a petition under Section 3104 of California's Family Code, seeking court-ordered visitation.Timothy argued that he had developed an established relationship with the older granddaughter because he had cared for her for almost two years. He also alleged that Sarah had refused to let him visit the children. His petition requested one weekend visit and two dinnertime visits every month, along with weekly video calls. Sarah opposed the request, arguing that her father-in-law did not have a substantial relationship with the children that justified court-ordered visitation.Court allowed only a five-minute monthly telephone callWhile the long-term visitation dispute remained unresolved, the trial court issued an interim order allowing Timothy one telephone call with the children each month. The call was limited to five minutes. The court also scheduled a hearing to consider a longer-term visitation arrangement. Meanwhile, Sarah sought to recover the legal expenses she had incurred while fighting the grandfather's petition. She requested $17,193 in attorney's fees and costs.Of that amount, $7,193 represented expenses she had already paid when she submitted the request. She estimated that another $10,000 would be needed for continued preparation and proceedings. The trial court rejected her request, concluding that it did not have statutory authority to award attorney's fees in a grandparent visitation case. Sarah challenged that decision, arguing that the grandfather's petition fell under California's Uniform Parentage Act and that she was therefore entitled to financial assistance under Family Code Section 7605.Appeals court explains why the fee provision did not applyThe central question before the appellate court was whether Section 7605 could be used to recover legal expenses in a proceeding initiated by a grandparent seeking visitation. The provision allows courts to order one party to pay another party's attorney's fees in certain proceedings involving child custody, visitation and parentage under the Uniform Parentage Act.However, the appellate judges explained that Timothy had filed his petition under Section 3104, which specifically addresses grandparents' rights to seek visitation. That provision belongs to a different part of California's Family Code and is not included in the Uniform Parentage Act. The court therefore concluded that the grandfather's petition was not a proceeding under the Act and did not qualify for the fee-shifting provision.Sarah also argued that the visitation dispute should be treated as a proceeding arising from earlier parentage and custody judgments issued during the children's juvenile dependency cases. The appellate court rejected this argument as well. It explained that juvenile dependency proceedings and Uniform Parentage Act cases serve different legal purposes. Dependency proceedings are initiated to protect children who may be at risk of harm and involve decisions about custody, parental rights and family reunification.Although the juvenile court had made parentage determinations and issued custody and visitation orders, those decisions were made under juvenile law. They did not automatically become judgments under the Uniform Parentage Act simply because the court used certain parentage standards.Court affirmed denial of the $17,193 requestAfter examining both arguments, the California Court of Appeal found no legal basis for requiring Timothy to pay Sarah's attorney's fees and costs under Section 7605. The judges concluded that the trial court had correctly interpreted the law and had not abused its discretion by rejecting the request.The appellate court therefore affirmed the order denying Sarah's application for $17,193. It also directed both parties to bear their own costs of the appeal. Importantly, the appeal concerned the mother's request for legal expenses, not a final determination of the grandfather's long-term visitation rights. The five-minute monthly telephone call was an interim arrangement while the wider visitation dispute was being addressed.The November 3 ruling thus settled the question of whether the mother could recover her legal expenses under the particular statutory provision, without deciding the merits of the grandfather's request for regular visits.You use AI every day. articles.title: California Gov. Gavin Newsom plans to commute all death sentences
articles.summary: Gov. Gavin Newsom said Thursday that he intends to commute all California death sentences, declaring that “state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with” values in America’s most populous state.
articles.body: Gov. Gavin Newsom said Thursday that he intends to commute all California death sentences, declaring that “state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with” values in America’s most populous state. In an open letter to constituents, Newsom said taking this step is “among the most difficult of my career.” “I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values,” he said. California has not put a prisoner to death since Jan. 17, 2006, when Clarence Ray Allen was executed via lethal injection. Newsom said his executive action would impact the “548 people now under death sentence in California,” making for “the largest death row in the Western Hemisphere.” The move, however, requires the state Supreme Court to approve resentencing in those cases where the person has more than one felony conviction, which Newsom said amounts to 382 of the prisoners on death row. “I respectfully request that the Court issue its recommendation by the end of this year so that I may act before the end of my term,” Newsom, who is term-limited and leaves office in January, wrote in a letter Thursday to the justices. There were 561 inmates on death row as of Tuesday, according to Department of Corrections records. In 2019, when there were 737 inmates awaiting execution in the state, Newsom ordered a moratorium on all of those cases. In a statement at the time, he said the death penalty was discriminatory, provided no public safety benefit and wasted billions. Richard Allen Davis, who was convicted in the murder of 12-year-old Polly Klaas in 1993, is one of the inmates still on California’s death row. Klaas had been abducted at knifepoint from her home in Petaluma, north of San Francisco, during a slumber party. The case drew national attention after it triggered a massive search that eventually led investigators to Davis, who then directed police to the girl’s body in a shallow grave. Marc Klaas, Polly’s father, said Newsom’s decision is a “knife in the back” to him and other victims’ families who believe death row prisoners were lawfully sentenced. “It’s unbelievably disappointing,” Klaas told NBC News. “I was told that when this guy was sentenced to death that this was a system we can trust. But here we are, 33 years later, and it’s a system we can’t trust.” Newsom’s proposal was embraced by death penalty abolitionists, human rights advocates and faith communities. “This is a day that will be remembered in California’s history and resonate globally for years to come,” Amnesty International USA Executive Director Nadia Daar said in a statement. “The death penalty should be abolished, everywhere. Today marks a significant moment for human rights in California and across the country,” Daar said. The president of the National Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers cited “countless” studies that she said show that the death penalty doesn’t deter crime and called the move a “decision of historic moral clarity and courage.” “The death penalty is unjust, uncivilized, and inconsistent with the fallibility of our justice system,” Melissa “Missy” Owen said in a statement. Since the U.S. Supreme Court ended a brief pause in capital punishment with its landmark 1976 ruling in Gregg v. Georgia, there have been 1,687 state executions, according to Death Penalty Information Center records. Texas has carried out the most executions in that time, 603, while California has carried out a death sentence just 13 times. “Governor Newsom’s announcement marks a decisive moment in the history of the death penalty in the United States,” Death Penalty Information Center Executive Director Robin Maher said in statement. “Though other governors have granted universal clemencies, none have been at this scale.” Newsom, a Democrat, is frequently mentioned as a possible presidential candidate for 2028, and the timing of this announcement isn’t lost on Klaas. “We’re talking about serial killers, we’re talking about spree killers, we’re talking about cop killers, we’re talking about child killers,” Klaas said. “Why, two days after the midterms, does Gavin Newsom feel the need to commute these sentences? Who benefits from this?” In a statement, the California District Attorney’s Association condemned Newsom’s decision, saying the governor replaced individual sentencing decisions that were reached after extensive legal proceedings “with a single executive decision that makes no distinction among the crimes committed, the circumstances of the offenders or the victims whose lives were taken.” “With the stroke of a pen, Governor Newsom has disregarded the decisions of hundreds of jurors and judges, and the anguish of families who lost loved ones to the worst crimes imaginable,” said Monterey County District Attorney and association president Jeannine M. Pacioni. San Luis Obispo County District Attorney Dan Dow said Newsom’s action is an affront to the families of victims, whose killers were brought to justice by his office. “Governor Newsom just told the families of Rachel Newhouse, Aundria Crawford, Kesha Gurke and every other innocent victim of California’s 548 condemned killers that the killers’ lives matter more,” Dow said in statement as immediate past president of the California District Attorneys Association. “Juries chose justice case by case, voters chose it five times, and one outgoing governor is trying to erase it all with a pen. This is a sickening abuse of power.”

articles.title: Top US civil rights official resigns
articles.summary: New Democratic Congress expected to probe Trump Justice Department office’s handling of Epstein files and ICE killings.
articles.body:
As President Donald Trump’s administration prepares for a flurry of congressional investigations into shootings by immigration agents and the Jeffrey Epstein files, the top official in charge of the United States Department of Justice’s civil rights division has resigned.

US Attorney General Todd Blanche on Thursday confirmed Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon’s departure in a post on social media.

“Today, I accepted the resignation of Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon,” Blanche wrote on X. “She has defended the civil liberties of every American and enforced the law without fear or favor.”

A top Trump ally, Dhillon was confirmed to her role in April 2025 and has overseen a dramatic overhaul of the Justice Department’s civil rights division, which is tasked with enforcing anti-discrimination laws. Hundreds of former Justice Department officials penned a letter last December decrying the “destruction” of the agency division under Trump.

Dhillon is the first high-ranking official to resign from the Trump administration since US Democrats swept both chambers of the US Congress in the country’s pivotal midterm elections on Tuesday.

Democratic congressman Robert Garcia, who will likely become the new chair of the powerful House of Representatives Committee on Oversight and Accountability, pledged on Wednesday to take on four major investigations, including abuses of power by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents and the Epstein files.

Dhillon reportedly told her staff earlier this year that her office, which has typically been charged with investigating law enforcement killings by police officers, would not be looking into the fatal shootings of two US citizens – Renee Good and Alex Pretti – who were gunned down by ICE agents in Minneapolis.

In May, Garcia accused the administration of continuing to shield Trump from scrutiny related to unreleased documents tied to the Epstein investigation

During a closed-door hearing in which Blanche’s predecessor, Pam Bondi, was asked by lawmakers about the case, the California Democrat Garcia alleged Dhillon repeatedly intervened to block questions about the president’s connection to the release of the files.

The Justice Department referred Al Jazeera to Blanche’s social media post when asked when Dhillon submitted her resignation. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

articles.title: Who could be behind hoax bomb threats to European air travel?
articles.summary: There is no hard evidence so far linking airline bomb threats to Russia, Iran or any proxy groups.
articles.body:
The warnings came in thick and fast, targeting one airline or airport after another.

In nearly all cases - London's Heathrow airport being a notable exception - they were taken to be credible enough to divert the aircraft in question, or even in Italy's case, to scramble fighter jets to escort it.

They all turned out to be false, which does not, of course, mean that the next ones will not be real.

It is hardly surprising that the simultaneous, co-ordinated nature of these airline hoaxes, coupled with other malicious actions across Europe, are causing some people to point the finger of suspicion at Russia.

Following a series of cyber-attacks and mysterious drone sightings over sensitive sites earlier this year, in the past few days we have seen the remote hacking of supermarket freezers, as well as a blood bank, a suspicious incident on Poland's border with Russia, and in August a drone attack Germany's Leipzig Halle airport which its interior minister publicly blamed on Moscow.

There are many who argue, based purely on circumstantial evidence, that this must surely be yet another example of "hybrid", "grey zone" or "sub-threshold" warfare - actions that damage a nation's infrastructure or society but which tend to be anonymous, deniable and which fall short of triggering Nato's Article 5 and thereby mobilising a response by the West.

Moscow is certainly furious with Nato for supporting Ukraine and, in doing so, frustrating the Kremlin's plans to swallow up that country and effectively terminate its independence.

Russian bloggers have also suggested that, if Ukraine's drones are currently making Russia's airports unsafe, and Western sanctions are blocking Russian airlines from European airspace, then why shouldn't Western nations feel the same pain?

But as of Thursday evening no hard evidence had emerged linking the airline hoaxes to Russia, Iran or any proxy groups controlled by them.

There is the email threat sent on Thursday morning to airport authorities in Rome, purporting to be from "Fighters of the Male State".

That name likely refers to the Russian group Muzhskoi Legion or "Male Legion", an ultra-right group with such extreme views it was banned by a Moscow court in 2021.

Yet, it retained tens of thousands of online followers on Telegram as it cheered on the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine in the following year.

But the email sent to Rome, even if genuine - and who is to say it is not another group hiding behind that name? - is unlikely to provide the leads that police and airport authorities need to pin down who is generating these hoaxes and why.

For national police forces, airport authorities and transport ministries trying to work out who is behind these hoaxes and how best to mitigate their effect when they happen again, the task is not to go with who they think might be the most likely culprits but instead to follow the cold, hard leads - if they can find them.

articles.title: The blame game: How the US midterm shock is shaping Israel’s race for PM
articles.summary: The Republican midterm rout is helping shape who leads Israel next, as Netanyahu’s US ties turn toxic.
articles.body:
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has long sold himself as the leader who will ensure that ties with the United States, the country’s most important ally, remain strong. The endorsement he received in the run-up to Israel’s parliamentary elections last month from US President Donald Trump added to that perception, in the same year as Washington and Tel Aviv jointly went to war against Iran.

Then came the US midterm elections, and the disastrous performance of Trump’s Republican Party. Early analysis of why the Republicans lost so badly has in part focused on that war with Iran, and the United States’s relationship with Israel. Both were highlighted by US Vice President JD Vance.

Suddenly, Netanyahu’s argument that he is the US-Israel relationship’s secret sauce looks much weaker. If anything, it can be argued that Netanyahu, and his policies – resulting in a genocidal war in Gaza, the Iran war, and numerous attacks in the wider region – have made Israel politically toxic in the US.

Many Israelis are now worried that the country can no longer rely on unquestioned support from the US. And as Israel’s political leaders jockey to try and form a government following the parliamentary elections, the opposition has laid the blame squarely at Netanyahu’s feet, and argued that it is another reason he should not be allowed to form the next government.

Yair Lapid, a former Israeli prime minister whose party is a member of the bloc seeking to unseat Netanyahu, stressed his own ties to members of the US Congress in a social media post. He added that he believed US voters were not so much against Israel as “against extremist ministers who say crazy things. They’re against settler violence; they’re against a government they don’t understand; they’re mainly against Netanyahu — for them, anything connected to him is toxic”.

Avigdor Lieberman, another opposition leader, echoed what many in Israel are said to suspect : that Trump’s election-day announcement that US military aid to Israel would end had been traded for his endorsement of the prime minister. “The price of Trump’s support for Netanyahu – $3.8bn dollars a year,” Lieberman wrote on social media.

“With America stopping the money it has channelled to Israel for so many years, the defence budget, already 7 percent of GDP, will have to rise. Israelis will feel it in their pocket. But then, you can’t be a rogue state and expect things to continue as before,” Ahron Bregman, an Israeli security analyst and senior teaching fellow at King’s College London, said. “In Israel, Netanyahu continues to do what he has always done so well, turning one segment of the population against the other. He’s now trying to delegitimise the Arabs by saying they stole the elections, in order to stop the opposition having the Arabs as partners.”

Israel’s general election on October 27 left Netanyahu’s right-wing bloc with 53 seats in parliament, eight short of the 61 needed to form a government.

The opposition bloc led by former army chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot got 48 seats, while the Arab-led parties – the United Arab List (Ra’am) and the Joint List – have 19 seats. The Arab-led parties have both said that they will support Eisenkot for prime minister.

Eisenkot and other opposition leaders have rejected suggestions of a unity government with Netanyahu, leaving him without a clear path to a majority.

It is now up to Israeli President Isaac Herzog to nominate a politician to form a government, but he has yet to do so.

As things stand, Eisenkot’s self-styled Zionist bloc, which has previously ruled out serving alongside the Arab-led parties, stands to benefit from their backing from outside the government, despite Netanyahu’s attacks.

Eisenkot’s prospects were boosted further on Thursday when United Torah Judaism (UTJ), Netanyahu’s longtime ultra-Orthodox ally, declined for the first time since 2009 to recommend him or anyone else to form a government, an apparent defection that weakens the prime minister’s position while giving a boost to his opponents.

But Eisenkot replacing Netanyahu as Israel’s prime minister does not necessarily mean that he will be able to reverse Israel’s declining popularity in the US. An April Pew Research Center poll suggested that public attitudes in the US are as negative towards Israel as they are towards Netanyahu, noted pollster Shibley Telhami, the director of the University of Maryland Critical Issues Poll.

“Our own poll found that most Americans would not change their view of Israel, even if there is a new government without Netanyahu,” said Telhami. “Any government of Israel would be swimming against the rising public tide … I don’t think any government of Israel could return relations back to where they were five years ago.”

articles.summary: Sheriff Andy Rohrich said college students Kaden Matsuda and Jackson Donlon died instantly and did not suffer in the West Apostle Mountain climbing accident.
articles.body: Authorities have identified the likely cause of a fatal fall that killed two college students in the Colorado mountains last week, saying a rock securing their rappelling equipment likely gave way during their descents. Kaden Matsuda, 19, and Jackson Donlon, 20 — both students at Colorado Mountain College — were found dead in a snow-filled basin on West Apostle Mountain, roughly 100 miles southeast of Aspen. They had failed to return from a weekend climbing trip, according to The Associated Press (AP). The two were rappelling down the mountain when the accident occurred, according to findings released this week by the Chaffee County Sheriff's Office. ONE MAN TURNED A GLOBAL SKYSCRAPER INTO HIS MOST DANGEROUS DESTINATION OF ALL: 'PRETTY SURREAL' Donlon was beginning his descent from an anchor point backed up by additional safety protections when the rock likely gave way, authorities said on Tuesday. Matsuda was attached to the same anchor, causing both students to fall. Investigators have not determined exactly how far they plunged, AP said. The pair had set out from the college's Leadville campus, initially planning to climb nearby Ice Mountain before apparently changing their destination to West Apostle Mountain, according to authorities. Autopsies determined that both students died instantly from multiple blunt force injuries, while authorities said the severe snowstorm was not a direct factor in their deaths. THOUSANDS SWARM STUNNING MOUNTAIN ESCAPE AS SELFIE TOURISM BACKLASH ERUPTS ONLINE Investigators found no obvious mistakes in the students' preparation for the climb, according to the Chaffee County Sheriff's Office. "In most similar cases that have led to a devastating conclusion we find it easy to pick apart what was done wrong," Chaffee County Sheriff Andy Rohrich said, according to AP. "That was not the case with Kaden and Jackson." Rohrich also expressed relief that neither student suffered in their final moments. AMERICAN TOURIST FALLS 1,000 FEET TO HER DEATH WHILE CHASING PERFECT MOUNTAIN PHOTO "While their lives were far too short, they spent their final moments together surrounded by the majestic beauty of Chaffee County’s high peaks that they loved," he said. articles.summary: Interception comes after Saudi civil defence agency warned of potential danger near the strategic port of Yanbu.
articles.body:
The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen’s Houthis has said it intercepted a ballistic missile fired by the Iran-aligned armed group towards the Medina region, home to one of Islam’s holiest cities.

The announcement on Thursday came just minutes after Saudi Arabia’s civil defence agency warned of potential danger in the area near the strategic port of Yanbu.

“Air defence intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia toward the Medina region,” coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki said in a post on X.

The Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), have rejected any suggestion they were targeting the city, saying such accusations were a “blatant and grave falsehood”.

Houthi Military spokesman Yahya Saree wrote on X that “our operations target only oil facilities and military bases” and called the allegation a lie.

Among their attacks on airports, energy infrastructure and military sites, the Houthis have targeted the port of Yanbu on several occasions in recent months.

“A warning has been issued by the National Early Warning Platform in Yanbu Governorate to alert of a potential danger,” read a statement published by the agency online.

The agency later announced that the threat had passed.

Yanbu is a ⁠⁠major oil export hub ⁠⁠and a ⁠⁠key ⁠⁠outlet for oil shipments ‌‌transported through the kingdom’s ‌‌East-West ‌‌pipeline.

The port and pipeline have played a key role since the outbreak of the United States-Israeli war on Iran in February, helping Riyadh ship crude and fuel to global markets.

Separately, Yemen’s internationally recognised government forces made gains in the Sanamat area in Taiz governorate, where fighting continues to rage .

Colonel Majed Abdullah al-Nazili said on Thursday that government forces carried out 1,298 “targeting operations” against the Houthis in the past 24 hours and “managed to gain control” of Sanamat.

The latest operations killed about 400 Houthi fighters and destroyed 132 vehicles, cars or heavy weapons placements, he said. Al Jazeera could not independently verify the claims.

Yemeni government forces previously reclaimed Taiz’s Dhubab district and key positions near the critical Bab al-Mandeb strait.

Meanwhile, on the al-Jawf front, military engineering units continue to clear recaptured sites of mines and booby traps, al-Nazili added.

Late last month, the government said 16,100 Houthi operatives and commanders had been killed or wounded since October 5.

The Houthis have not confirmed a death toll and have in the meantime been firing missiles regularly towards Saudi Arabia, hitting multiple airports and disrupting air traffic over the kingdom.

Yazeed al-Jeddawy, a research manager at the Sana’a Center for Strategic Studies, told Al Jazeera that the course of the conflict increasingly appears to be moving towards a prolonged war of attrition as the government offensive has not shifted the balance of power over the past 30 days.

“The conflict is no longer driven solely by the dynamics inside Yemen; it is intertwined with the wider regional confrontation and the war involving Iran,” he added.

articles.title: Hundreds of thousands march in France’s biggest day of protests in years. Here’s what we know
articles.summary: About 575,000 protesters participated in demonstrations across France on Thursday, according to government estimates, marking the biggest single day of protests since a wave of unrest began in September to coincide with a nationwide strike.
articles.body: About 575,000 protesters participated in demonstrations across France on Thursday, according to government estimates, marking the biggest single day of protests since a wave of unrest began in September to coincide with a nationwide strike. Despite the scale of these protests, and the violence which marred similar marches on October 17, the day passed relatively peacefully, albeit with some localized clashes in cities across France. Some workers went on strike too, depleting some schools, universities, railways and, to a lesser extent, hospitals of their staff. The diverse nature of sectors involved reflects just how many groups are now participating in these protests, which have expanded from students demanding better conditions in schools to a movement that has drawn in trade unions and Yellow Vest protesters. Each group has its own concerns, though they are united by widespread discontent over the cost of living, perceived government inaction, a growing wealth divide and a deep desire for social and political change. What was the impact of the strikes? Several of France’s biggest unions, representing everyone from students, teachers and postal workers to doctors, pharmacists and transport workers had called for a nationwide strike today. About one in three of France’s higher education institutions were “disrupted” because of the demonstrations, while about 13% of all school staff went on strike, the government estimated. The unions estimated far larger numbers. Some train services were also disrupted because of striking workers. Very few public hospital staff — only about 5% of the workforce — participated in the strike, France’s health ministry told CNN. “No significant disruption to healthcare services has been reported,” the ministry added. Were the protests violent? Ever since protests turned violent almost three weeks ago, authorities and shopkeepers have braced for similar scenes at every one of these nationwide demonstrations. However, the day passed without major incident, aside from “clashes between police and groups of radical and far-left activists in several cities, including Rennes, Nannes, Lyon and Marseille,” France’s Interior Ministry said. Altogether, police detained 448 people. In Lyon, police fired tear gas and charged a group of protesters, many of them masked while “several dozen” agitators were arrested in Rennes after they vandalized a hotel, threw objects at police and “violently attacked” protesting union members, authorities said. One school near Toulouse was badly damaged by a “deliberate act of arson,” according to French education minister Édouard Geffray, and firefighters responded to 86 fires across the country, the Interior Ministry said. Laurent Nuñez, the interior minister, said: “In a context where, once again, numerous acts of violence occurred, law enforcement officers responded with courage and determination to ensure that the right to protest could be exercised peacefully and safely, despite the controversial claims accusing them of obstructing it.” What are the protesters demanding? Each group involved in these protests has slightly different demands. The labour unions which called for a strike today are demanding higher wages and pensions. In particular, the CGT, one of France’s most prominent unions, says the minimum wage must increase immediately by 10%. Another union — the CFDT — is demanding a 100 euro, about 7%, increase in the minimum monthly wage. Student groups, meanwhile, are demanding an increase of more than $10 billion in the education budget, as well as a $1.5 billion investment in school infrastructure and 250,000 additional university places. The Gilets Jaunes or Yellow Vests — a radical movement that first emerged eight years ago — is demanding the departure of President Emmanuel Macron and his government, and a new constitutional process. Will the protests continue? In short, yes. None of these demands are easily attainable and protesters are indicating their intention to keep demonstrating until Christmas, and possibly even until France’s presidential elections next spring. Even just looking ahead to the next few days, the Yellow Vests are planning to protest on Friday and Saturday. Elsewhere in Europe, where similar protest movements have emerged, strikes are planned later this month in Spain, Italy, Portugal and Belgium. How are authorities handling the protests? Stung by being caught unawares on October 17, authorities have remained “extremely vigilant” in their preparation for these protests, a government spokesperson said Wednesday, according to Reuters. But while security forces on the ground have largely managed to stifle any violence, Macron has been criticized for failing to adequately respond to the protesters’ demands. “I want high schools to be able to reopen after the holiday because, when we talk about the future of our young people, they need to be able to return to class,” he told French journalist and YouTuber HugoDécrypte. He argued that young people “have been heard,” and called for them to “return to class, for calm to be restored and for high schools to reopen under proper conditions,” even as they continue protesting.

articles.title: South Africa’s ANC on track for new lows in local polls
articles.summary: The ANC was on about 32 percent of the vote with more than 60 percent of votes counted in municipal elections.
articles.body:
South Africa’s early municipal election results have shown the African National Congress (ANC) with a sharply reduced vote share, weakening the long-dominant party’s control of key cities such as Johannesburg.

The ANC was on about 32 percent of the vote, with the Democratic Alliance (DA) in second place at 25 percent, after more than 60 percent of the votes had been counted in this week’s municipal elections, data from the election commission showed late on Thursday.

Meanwhile, former President Jacob Zuma’s breakaway opposition uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) party was in third place with 8.5 percent, below levels suggested by opinion polls.

About 15.9 million of 29.2 million registered voters cast ballots, the electoral commission said, putting turnout at an estimated 54.5 percent, up from 46 percent in the pandemic-hit 2021 local elections.

The ANC, which has been South Africa’s largest party since it led the country out of apartheid in 1994, has tended to do worse in municipal elections than nationally and has acknowledged its failures in local governance.

From nearly 70 percent of the national vote in 2004, the ANC fell below 50 percent for the first time in the 2021 municipal elections, winning 46 percent.

At the 2024 national elections, it managed just more than 40 percent and was forced to accept a unity government with nine other parties, including the DA.

The party, now led by President Cyril Ramaphosa, has borne the brunt of criticism about years of municipal mismanagement that have left South Africans grappling with failing water supplies, persistent power cuts and crumbling public services.

It has also faced corruption allegations, while splinter parties have eaten away at its support base.

The results of this week’s local ballot will offer a key measure of voters’ sentiment ahead of the 2029 general election.

Control of the country’s eight major metropolitan municipalities is up for grabs, alongside dozens of district and local councils.

The MK party had been tipped as one of the few parties capable of securing an outright majority in the eastern port city of Durban.

But projections by the Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR), a state-funded research body, put its support there at 32 percent.

The DA, meanwhile, was forecast to retain control of tourist magnet Cape Town with 56 percent of the vote, with its leader, Geordin Hill-Lewis, already declaring victory.

The party was also leading with 34 percent in Johannesburg, the country’s financial capital, after running a spirited campaign spearheaded by its former leader, Helen Zille, 75, according to CSIR projections.

With outright majorities far from assured in several major cities, the results could usher in another round of complex coalition negotiations, with parties bargaining to assemble the alliances needed to govern.
