articles.title: Qualcomm co-founder Irwin Jacobs pledges $50 million to build over 500 affordable homes for homeless people in San Diego, including 150 units for seniors
articles.summary: San Diego is set to get more than 500 affordable homes for people experiencing homelessness following a major financial commitment from Qualcomm
articles.body: San Diego is set to get more than 500 affordable homes for people experiencing homelessness following a major financial commitment from Qualcomm co-founder Irwin Jacobs. As reported by KPBS, in September 2026, Jacobs pledged $50 million to Father Joe’s Villages, marking the largest donation in the organisation’s history. The funding will support a $300 million-plus redevelopment project in downtown San Diego, featuring three residential towers, 77 shelter rooms and dedicated accommodation for older residents. With 150 homes planned for seniors, the development will also include support programmes covering assisted living, healthcare and hospice care, with completion targeted for 2032.Irwin Jacobs makes his largest donation to Father Joe’s VillagesThe $50 million pledge is the largest single donation Father Joe’s Villages has received in its history. Jacobs, who co-founded telecommunications company Qualcomm, announced the commitment in September 2026 as the organisation prepared for a major expansion of its housing facilities.The money will contribute towards the development of the Joan and Irwin Jacobs Family Campus, a proposed residential and support complex at the organisation's existing headquarters in downtown San Diego. According to KPBS reports, the project is expected to cost more than $300 million.Deacon Jim Vargas, the organisation's president and chief executive, said the contribution would help move the project beyond its early planning stages. The funds are also expected to establish resources for predevelopment work and construction deposits, allowing the organisation to advance the project more quickly.Three residential towers planned for downtown San DiegoThe proposed campus will be built on the site of the existing Joan Kroc Center, near the intersection of Imperial Avenue and 15th Street. Rather than retaining the current building, the organisation plans to demolish it and replace it with three residential towers. Each tower is expected to stand approximately 10 storeys tall. Together, the buildings are planned to provide more than 500 affordable housing units, alongside 77 rooms for shelter accommodation.The development is intended to serve people who need longer-term affordable homes as well as those requiring temporary shelter. Its location will also allow residents to access the support services already associated with Father Joe’s Villages.The existing Joan Kroc Center has operated as a place of temporary accommodation and assistance for people experiencing homelessness for decades. Its facilities include housing and support services, while healthcare provision, including dental and behavioural health services, is available nearby.Why 150 homes will be reserved for older residentsAn important part of the proposed development concerns people aged 55 and above. Of the more than 500 affordable units planned for the campus, 150 are expected to be reserved for senior residents. The decision reflects the age profile of homelessness in the San Diego area. According to the latest local count cited by Father Joe’s Villages, approximately one in three people experiencing homelessness were aged 55 or older.For this group, housing difficulties can overlap with health problems, limited income and the need for ongoing assistance. People who have spent years without permanent accommodation may also require services that go beyond providing a room or an apartment.Vargas explained that the organisation wanted to address needs that are not always covered by conventional homelessness programmes. These include assisted living arrangements, hospice care and support for people nearing the end of their lives.The proposed senior care programme is also expected to include case management and employment services. Such assistance would allow the organisation to address practical challenges faced by older residents, including access to healthcare and help managing their daily circumstances.The donation will support services beyond housingJacobs's contribution is not intended to fund residential construction alone. Part of the commitment will also help Father Joe’s Villages develop programmes for senior residents who need additional care.The organisation has identified assisted living and hospice services as areas requiring attention. Older people living on the streets may have health conditions that have gone untreated or deteriorated over time. Some may need end-of-life support that traditional emergency shelter facilities are not equipped to provide. This creates a different set of requirements for organisations working with homelessness. Providing accommodation can address an immediate need, but older residents may also require medical assistance, care coordination and support with everyday activities.San Diego officials point to growing housing pressureThe proposed campus comes at a time when local officials are facing continued demand for affordable accommodation. County Supervisor Paloma Aguirre, whose district includes the area where the redevelopment is planned, spoke about the difficulties residents are experiencing as living costs rise. She said concerns about housing insecurity are increasingly being raised by constituents, including people living on fixed incomes who face the possibility of losing their housing or struggling to maintain access to healthcare.San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria also addressed the project at a press conference announcing the donation. He said the average review period for affordable housing developments in the city had fallen to nine days, compared with a process that previously could take years.The city is working to speed up the necessary approvals for the Father Joe’s Villages redevelopment. Aguirre said efforts to shorten the permitting process were intended to prevent administrative delays from affecting the construction schedule.Construction is expected to begin in 2028The redevelopment will require changes for people currently staying at the Joan Kroc Center. Father Joe’s Villages expects to relocate temporary residents in early 2028 so the existing building can be cleared ahead of construction. Those residents are expected to move to the organisation's Tucson Campus on Fifth Avenue and Ash Street. Vargas said they would continue receiving the same services during the relocation period and would be brought back once the new facilities are ready.The organisation's current schedule calls for construction of the first tower to begin in 2028. Work on the second is expected to start towards the end of that year, followed by the third tower in 2029. The full Joan and Irwin Jacobs Family Campus is targeted for completion in 2032. These dates remain part of the project's current plan and may depend on fundraising, approvals and construction progress.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A moderate millennial newcomer could decide knife-edge New Zealand election
articles.summary: New Zealand is set for one of its tightest elections in years, with the incumbent conservative coalition facing an uncertain path to power and polls pointing to a millennial newcomer becoming the kingmaker.
articles.body: New Zealand is set for one of its tightest elections in years, with the incumbent conservative coalition facing an uncertain path to power and polls pointing to a millennial newcomer becoming the kingmaker. Support for two parties that have dominated Wellington politics for almost a century – the center-right National party and center-left Labour party – has cratered below 30% respectively in public polling, with voters turning to players entrenched further to the right, the left, and to a centrist party that could enter parliament for the first time. Frustrated with soaring living costs, stubbornly high unemployment and a stagnant economy in recent years, voters on Saturday are looking beyond their traditional choices. Shaking up the race is the centrist Opportunity party, led by Qiulae Wong, an articulate 38-year-old former sustainable business consultant and mother of two, who goes by ‘Q’ for short. She entered politics just a year ago by responding to a job advertisement for the party’s leadership role. Her party, pitching itself as both business and climate friendly and promising a land tax as well as a universal basic income to replace welfare payments, looks set to secure enough votes to cross the 5% threshold required to secure seats in parliament, on current polling. That would make it the first total outsider party (not involving established political figures) to do so in 30 years –– a “super significant” feat according to Lara Greaves, an associate professor in politics at Wellington’s Victoria University. “There’s not been really anything like it, and we’ve seen a number of well-funded attempts,” she told CNN, explaining that the party was finding appeal with people “frustrated with the status quo.” If Saturday’s results mirror the polls, Opportunity would hold the balance of power – with both the incumbent right and the opposition left coalition groupings in need of their support to secure a majority. Effectively, that means Wong could have her choice of government, and her party is happy to work with either side. But Prime Minister Christopher Luxon, who leads the right-wing National-led coalition government, has already ruled out a post-election deal with Opportunity. He may yet face the stark choice of walking that back or losing power. Neither Luxon, who faced-down two caucus confidence votes in his leadership this year, nor his key opponent Labour’s Chris Hipkins (a former prime minister himself) have been able to endear themselves to the public like former leaders Jacinda Ardern and John Key. Their relative unpopularity has shattered a decadeslong trend of battle royale-style campaigns between the major party leaders, giving the minor party contenders more attention and putting them in a position to have significant influence over the direction of the next government. Coalitions are a near constant under the South Pacific nation’s mixed-member proportional (MMP) voting system, but the minor parties have traditionally been supporting players, being granted a tiny proportion of cabinet posts and limited policy concessions. The powerful position the minor parties find themselves in this year is “unprecedented territory,” says Greaves. “This is going to be the first time we’re going to see these coalition agreements where the minor parties are really going to be saying: ‘Hey, we got a big chunk of the vote. You have to stop treating us like children.’” But that makes it “really hard to know what you’re voting for,” she said, explaining that fringe policies that get little attention during the campaign can ultimately end up on the government’s agenda after negotiations. The incumbent National-led coalition – New Zealand’s most right-wing government in a generation – could be pushed further to the right by its emboldened partners, who have touted deepening Culture War-style policies at times on the campaign trail. For example, the right-wing-libertarian ACT party has vowed to end affirmative action schemes at the country’s medical schools, while the nationalist New Zealand First party has promised sweeping immigration changes and its populist leader Winston Peters has voiced support for a review of the ban on gay conversion therapy. “With the 2023 government, a lot of people argue that that was already a huge lurch to the right, especially in terms of (indigenous) Māori rights… So that’s potentially concerning for more moderate voters,” said Greaves. Conversely, parties on the right have warned voters would face a raft of new taxes if a leftist coalition were able to form a government – with Labour promising a capital gains tax, and the leftist Greens touting taxes on the “super rich” and big tech companies who take New Zealand earned profits overseas. “If the left bloc were to win, they would have this real concern about exactly how they get the money to do what they want to do,” said Greaves. In recent decades, New Zealand elections have typically been easy to predict, but even the experts are struggling to foresee what voters will deliver on Saturday. “What’s going to happen? No idea,” said Greaves. Should Luxon’s National-led coalition lose, it will become the first single-term New Zealand government in more than half a century.

articles.title: Massachusetts college shut down in 2019 and lost nonprofit status in 2022, yet former student who left in 2009 owing $10,000 was sued for $28,000 in unpaid tuition and interest in 2025
articles.summary: Newbury College in Massachusetts shut its doors in 2019 and ceased operating as a nonprofit organisation in 2022.
articles.body: Newbury College in Massachusetts shut its doors in 2019 and ceased operating as a nonprofit organisation in 2022. However, its closure did not bring an end to its financial dealings with former students. In the summer of 2025, former student Cesarina Barros was sued for $28,000 in unpaid tuition and interest, raising questions about who collects outstanding fees when a college ceases to exist.According to a report by WGBH, Barros left Newbury College in 2009 because she could no longer afford her education. At the time, she owed approximately $10,000 in tuition but continued making payments towards the outstanding amount. When the institution eventually closed, she believed she would no longer have to worry about the debt.That changed when she received notice of the lawsuit in 2025. Barros, who now works as a registration specialist for Boston Public Schools, is among 21 former students facing collection proceedings over unpaid tuition balances. Court documents filed in Boston Municipal Court also indicate that former students have been threatened with wage garnishment.Where does the money collected from former students go?The case has raised an unusual question: if a college has shut down, who is legally entitled to collect the money former students owe, and where does that money ultimately go?During a court hearing, Barros asked Judge Steven Kim where the money collected from former students would go. However, neither the judge nor the lawyer representing Newbury College could provide an answer. The judge subsequently postponed the case until January.The uncertainty is particularly striking because Newbury's remaining assets were legally transferred to another educational institution.In 2022, Massachusetts' highest court and the state attorney general's office designated Wheaton College as the legal recipient of Newbury College's assets and funds. However, Wheaton spokesperson Suzi Robinson told WGBH that the institution did not acquire Newbury's student accounts or outstanding balances.Despite this clarification, collection filings reportedly list addresses associated with both Wheaton College and Newbury College. Wheaton also confirmed that an inherited scholarship fund worth approximately $4 million has supported seven students.Legal experts question collecting tuition from students after a college closesThe case has also prompted questions about whether former students should be required to repay tuition when the institution they attended shuts down before they can complete their education.Attorney Adam Minsky, who represents student loan borrowers and their families, said he had rarely encountered such a situation in his 15 years of practice."It's not something that I tend to see in my practice, and it's not a situation that has come up, and I've been doing this work for 15 years," he told WGBH.Anna Anderson, a senior attorney at the National Consumer Law Center, said such cases were becoming "a bigger problem." She advised people facing collection lawsuits to consult an attorney immediately rather than ignore the proceedings. Debt collectors can potentially seek additional money through fees, wage garnishments and liens.Anderson also explained that whether tuition owed directly to a closed college must be repaid depends on how the institution's affairs are wound down and whether its debts are transferred to another entity. Separate discharge provisions apply to federal and private student loans.For Barros, the lawsuit has brought considerable emotional and financial stress. The mother of two, who works in Boston Public Schools, hopes to complete her degree in early childhood education but says the legal proceedings have caused sleepless nights and headaches.You use AI every day. articles.title: EC rejigs work, new officer to oversee ECINet functioning
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Election Commission has reallocated work among its deputy election commissioners (DEC) and directors-general in view of the recent
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Election Commission has reallocated work among its deputy election commissioners (DEC) and directors-general in view of the recent appointment of DEC Prakash Rajpurohit. DG (IT) Seema Khanna, who heads the division that manages the ECINet portal and application, will now put up all files regarding the IT/ICT and grievances divisions under her charge through senior DEC Pawan Kumar Sharma.Sources in the commission said Khanna - whose name cropped up after Indian Express reported on Sept 23, 2026, that election commissioners S S Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had objected to the alleged "centralisation" of ECINET, with access restricted for even authorised field officers - was earlier putting up these files through senior DEC Maneesh Garg, and before that through then DEC Sanjay Kumar.Though Garg had, while officiating as DEC (administration) during the leave period of DEC Bhanu Prakash Yeturu in July, issued a work allocation order that allowed Khanna to no longer route her files through then DEC Sanjay Kumar, this order was never implemented after the two election commissioners S S Sandhu and Vivek Joshi objected. This is recorded in the affidavit filed recently by EC in the Supreme Court."The work redistribution orders issued by the officer concerned were never implemented after the orders of the two commissioners, and the oversight of the IT division by the DEC was never actually withdrawn," EC said in the affidavit issued with approval of the full commission.Khanna, as a result, continued routing files through Sanjay Kumar, and after his stint with Election Commission ended, through Kumar's link officer Maneesh Garg.Under the work reallocation order dated Nov 4, Pawan Kumar Sharma will be the new deputy election commissioner in-charge of the IT/ICT as well as grievance/PGRS divisions, and Khanna would put up files of these divisions through him.Sandhu and Joshi had written separate letters to cabinet secretary T V Somanathan in July end, complaining about the working of senior Garg. In the near-identical letters, they said that Garg, soon after assuming charge as link officer of then DEC (administration) Yeturu, who was on leave, had issued an order regarding work allocation among senior DECs, DGs and equivalent officers, without discussing the revised allocation with the commission or the two election commissioners. This, Sandhu and Joshi said, was despite repeated oral instructions to all officers concerned against taking such actions without prior approval of the commission.The cabinet secretary had merely forwarded the election commissioners' letter to Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, apart from sending an acknowledgement to the two commissioners. As per the file noting furnished by the cabinet secretariat in reply to an RTI application by Commodore Lokesh Batra (Retd), it was stated that any action against Garg "at this stage may be inappropriate" as the letters were not sent by the commission as a whole. "It may also be construed as interference in the functioning of the constitutional body," it was stated.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.summary: Office-bearers from 12 states skipped event NEW DELHI: Indian Youth Congress has suspended over 300 office-bearers from the organisation for not showing
articles.body: Office-bearers from 12 states skipped eventNEW DELHI: Indian Youth Congress has suspended over 300 office-bearers from the organisation for not showing up for the 'Chalo Delhi' rally of INDIA bloc Sunday - a significant step to drive home the message that the outfit is serious about mass mobilisation in future.IYC sources said organisational office-bearers from assembly to the central level were directed to attend the rally with Rahul Gandhi as the face. They were also asked to mark their attendance on "With IYC" app. The assembly point for the march ahead of the rally was Minto Road crossing.After the rally, the organisation analysed the attendance and decided to suspend 300 office-bearers across 12 states who did not come and also did not log any reasons for their absention.However, the suspended members were told that they would be reinstated if they perform well in future.The leading state in suspensions is MP with over 60 office-bearers, followed by Rajasthan with 32. Gujarat, Jharkhand, UP central and east, Uttarakhand, and Telangana were the other states.IYC chief Uday Bhanu Chib said around 20,000 workers turned up for the Nov 1 rally, but some office-bearers were missing. "It was important to send a message that discipline is important, especially when ordinary members came in big numbers." IYC has around 45,000 office-bearers from central to the assembly level.Sources said members from only neighbouring states were asked to attend the rally."It is important to convey to the organisation that in the serious times we are in and in wake of the winds of change blowing in the country, it is not acceptable if there is even one absention. All youths will have to pitch in," Chib said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Firms told to publish salaries in job adverts ahead of new law
articles.summary: The goverment argues the change will help jobseekers and could help to prevent pay discrimination.
articles.body:
Businesses should publish salaries in job adverts now, the prime minister is telling firms, rather than wait for a new law to come in that will force them to do so.

The government is planning to make pay details compulsory in adverts, with legislation on the issue being brought forward "as soon as possible".

It argues the change will help jobseekers, particularly those applying for their first job, and could help prevent pay discrimination. However, one industry group said setting pay was a complex process and regulating adverts was not always suitable.

It comes a week after the UK's equality watchdog said employees should legally be able to find out what their colleagues are earning .

The Cabinet Office launched a consultation into pay and reducing discrimination in the summer, and the government said there had been "overwhelming support" for greater transparency, with 94% of respondents backing the move.

"Whether you're a young person starting out or a parent trying to support your family, you should know what a job pays before spending your time and effort applying for it," Andy Burnham said.

The government said the move was part of attempts to reduce the nearly one million young people not in education, employment or training - or "Neet" - ahead of the final report of the Milburn Review into youth inactivity, which is due in the coming weeks.

Publishing salary details upfront could "expose unjustified differences in pay, give workers greater confidence to challenge discrimination and prevent disagreements over pay escalating into disputes".

Employers in Europe will have to disclose the initial pay or range for new roles, which must either be included in a published job advert or shared before an interview.

According to data from UK jobs website Adzuna , 51% of the adverts on its site in September had salary information, but the proportion has been falling in recent years.

Adzuna co-founder Andrew Hunter said being open about pay "should be the norm, not the exception".

He added that employers who put a salary on a job advert "attract more applicants, and better-suited ones".

Previous research from the CIPD , an industry body for human resources managers, has indicated that the public sector and charities are more likely to reveal pay information that private firms, while pay ranges were more common than specific salaries.

But it found not all employers were "fully transparent", with pay ranges sometimes wider than £10,000.

CIPD chief executive Neil Carberry said that while, in principle, giving salary details was "a good thing", in practice it was "more complicated".

"There isn't always a single fixed figure, and employers will want to set pay based on a candidate's skills, experience and potential."

Carberry added the process was complex, saying that drafting job adverts is "best left to good employer practice rather than government regulation".

The government has said it will set out further details on what information will be required and how the legislation will be enforced "in due course".

Last week, the Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC), said publishing salaries in job adverts would be a "positive step".

It also said bosses should be required to respond to questionnaires about colleagues' pay to cut pay discrimination.

At present, employers do not have to respond to employee requests for salary information about their co-workers.

The EHRC also said employers should be prevented from asking about current salary when offering a job to stop a history of discrimination from continuing.

Employers in the UK are currently allowed to ask you how much you get paid in your current role, but applicants are under no obligation to tell them .

articles.title: Dolly Parton's Imagination Library relaunches in Wales
articles.summary: Children in parts of Wales will be posted a free book every month until their fifth birthday.
articles.body:
A scheme set up by late country singer Dolly Parton, which posts a free book to children every month until their fifth birthday, has relaunched in parts of Wales.

Parton, who died aged 80 in August , was inspired by her father who couldn't read or write.

She set up the Imagination Library in 1995 and it's been rolled out in countries across the world.

But the charity has previously struggled in Wales, and there are calls for the programme to be "properly funded" for children across the country.

The Welsh government said it was "committed" to offering library spaces in primary schools and it funded a variety of schemes "to encourage reading for pleasure".

There are three school communities in Swansea that will be part of the new programme - Clwyd, Brynmill and Llanrhidian primary schools - as well as Pencoed Primary School in Bridgend and a community in Risca near Newport.

The scheme is aimed at trying to help parents and their children to access books, especially during a cost-of-living crisis.

Becky, 38, from Swansea said her nine-month-old baby, Phoebe, will benefit from the programme.

"We love it, we think it's amazing. I've got another little girl as well, Faith, and since she was a baby, we've read to her, and she is thriving now," she said.

"She loves reading to us instead. We buy her books constantly, so having a new one every month, she'll be waiting for it in the post."

Mum-of-three, Diana Cune, 34, said she encouraged all her children to read.

"I always tell my girls that knowledge is power, and books are the key to unlock that," she said.

"We're extremely lucky and I think this is a marvellous project for our community. The kids are very fortunate to have this project rolled out here."

With funding from National Lottery Wales, the scheme was launched at Clwyd Primary School on Wednesday.

There were performances by school pupils, as well as a Welsh language rendition of Dolly Parton's hit, Jolene, by singer-songwriter Bronwen Lewis.

The bilingual song, featuring Dolly Parton herself , along with her niece Jada Star, was released last month.

It followed the revelation that Parton has Welsh links in Machynlleth, Powys.

"It feels like a series of events have led to this," said Bronwen Lewis.

"From me singing in Welsh with Dolly Parton, her understanding her Welsh ancestry before she passed, and now a relaunch. It's unbelievable."

Across the UK, Dolly Parton's Imagination Library has gifted nearly eight million free books to children since launching in 2007.

In Wales, all children under five living in the participating school catchment areas will be eligible to register.

'Not enough emphasis on reading in schools'

But the relaunch has sparked discussions around reading more generally.

Welsh Children's Laureate Nicola Davies has called for more funding and emphasis on reading in schools to improve educational outcomes, after the latest Pisa test results suggested Wales' performance had fallen further behind other UK nations.

"I would like to really see this programme being properly funded so that it could be in every part in Wales," she said.

"I don't think there is enough emphasis on reading, the National Curriculum for Wales hardly mentions reading for pleasure, and reading for pleasure has been proved by so much research to be absolutely central to supporting children's educational performance across all subjects.

"As we all know, the education results for Wales are not great. That means that we're not doing a good enough job for our young people, we're not supporting our young people.

"I think the fundamental problem in government is that education is seen as a cost, not an investment."

This initiative is being delivered through a partnership between The Dollywood Foundation UK and Community Focused Schools.

Helena Barrett-Duncan, regional director of the foundation, said she would also like to see the scheme rolled out to other communities.

"We want every child in the UK of course, but we would really love to bring this programme across Wales," she said.

"This is the beginning... the dream would be where every child in Wales would get this monthly gift of books."

"Dolly dreams big - she always did - and this whole programme is about making dreams come true."

She also said that the charity is exploring how to bring Welsh language provision to the programme, with one bilingual book already included.

The Welsh government said reading was "a central part of our curriculum" and schools played "an important role in how learners develop a lifelong love of reading".

"We remain committed to a library space in every primary school to encourage reading for pleasure," it said.

"Through our curriculum grants, we have provided funding for literacy projects, including Love Reading Cymru and the Summer Reading Challenge to encourage reading for pleasure. Our Ymgolli campaign also aims to inspire our young people to see the value of reading in all its forms."

articles.title: California governor commutes death sentences of 548 death row inmates
articles.summary: California Governor Gavin Newsom has moved to commute the death sentences of all 548 inmates on the state's death row to life imprisonment without the
articles.body: California Governor Gavin Newsom has moved to commute the death sentences of all 548 inmates on the state's death row to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole. However, the California Supreme Court will have the final say in 382 of the cases.“I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values, undermines the foundations of our legal system, and diminishes each of us,” Newsom said in a public letter on Thursday.The decision comes as Newsom prepares to leave office after eight years and considers a presidential run. A long-standing opponent of capital punishment, he imposed a moratorium on executions in California in 2019.His latest move followed what he described as a realisation of “the limits of what government can justly accomplish”.According to figures provided by Newsom's office, the commutations cover 529 men and 19 women. Under the state constitution, the California Supreme Court must approve clemency for anyone convicted of a felony more than once. This applies to 382 inmates, or about 70% of those affected.Death penalty decision draws criticism and supportCalifornia voters upheld capital punishment in ballot measures in 2012 and 2016. However, no execution has taken place in the state since 2006. California has the largest death row in the Western Hemisphere.Newsom said the decision was among the most difficult choices of his career because of its impact on victims' families.“As Governor, I alone bear responsibility for this decision and its impact, just as I alone would bear responsibility for each execution,” he wrote, according to news agency AP.The move drew criticism from victims' groups and prosecutors. Patricia Wenskunas, founder of the nonprofit Crime Survivors, called it “offensive” and “outrageous”.Steve Herr, whose son Sam was murdered in 2010, said he was “absolutely disgusted”. “When somebody commits such a heinous crime, they do not deserve to live,” he said, calling Newsom “an outright coward”.San Luis Obispo County District Attorney Dan Dow described the move as a “sickening abuse of power”. Orange County District Attorney Todd Spitzer also condemned it.The American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU), however, welcomed the decision. Its executive director, Anthony Romero, said: “These commutations reflect what justice demands: an end to a racist, error-prone, and inhumane punishment that has burdened California for far too long.”The ACLU is challenging the state's death penalty statute, alleging racial discrimination and unconstitutionality.You use AI every day. articles.title: The week in 41 photos
articles.summary: Take a look at 41 photos of the week from October 29 to November 5.
articles.body: A “blue wave” swept the United States on Election Day, with Democrats flipping control of both the House and Senate in a resounding and historic midterm victory.The results were a visceral rejection of President Donald Trump's actions in his second term. Republicans were washed out of power in places the party hadn’t lost in a generation — and sometimes more. Only twice in the last 50 years had control of both chambers changed in the same cycle.The exact sizes of the Democrats’ majorities are still yet to be determined as the final results are counted.History was also made in some gubernatorial races on Tuesday. Georgia Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms is set to become the first Black female governor in US history. US Rep. Byron Donalds, a Republican, was elected the first Black governor of Florida. And Gina Hinojosa was elected as the first Latina governor of Texas.Here are some of the stories that made headlines over the past week, as well as some photos that caught our eye.
